title: Match page: choose a structure
question: Three ways to lay out /match/[id] so it answers "should I tip against the Model?" first. The look is fixed by DESIGN.md; these differ in how the page is organised. Pick one, steer, or re-roll.

options.label: Three calls on one pitch
options.thesis: Model, bookies and Elo drop as markers on one big pitch bar, so a split shows as markers on opposite sides of halfway.
options.viewport: Compact board (call, kickoff), then one large pitch with Model 63 / Elo 54 / Bookies 45 markers and a plain line saying who disagrees, then team lists as a mirrored teamsheet: home left, jersey numbers down the halfway, away right.
options.risk: Three markers on one bar can crowd when the voices sit within a few points of each other.

raised.raise: Symmetry across the halfway line is the page's rule: every section below mirrors home left, away right.

options.label: The split, said plainly
options.thesis: A one-line verdict leads ("The Model backs Manly. The bookies back Brisbane."), then each voice gets its own pitch bar.
materials: tabs for Teams / Head to head
options.viewport: The verdict sentence at display size, then four labelled pitch bars (Model, Model without odds, Bookies' opening price, Elo), then tabs switching between team lists and head to head.
options.risk: Stacked bars repeat a lot of chrome; the verdict sentence must be generated well or it reads robotic.

options.label: The case for each side
options.thesis: Evidence is sorted by which team it backs: a panel for Sea Eagles and a panel for Broncos, each listing who backs them and why.
materials: two evidence panels in team colours
options.viewport: Compact board, then "The case for Sea Eagles" (Model 63%, Elo 54%, won the last meeting 34–6) and "The case for Broncos" (bookies 55%, 3 of the last 5), then team lists and the head-to-head table.
options.risk: Sorting evidence by side can feel like it argues both ways; the numbers have to stay neutral.
